clinicalPearls: A distinct B-cell entity separate from classic Hodgkin lymphoma, characterised by scattered lymphocyte-predominant (LP) or popcorn cells within a background of small B cells and follicular dendritic meshworks
The neoplastic LP cells retain the B-cell programme and are typically CD20-positive, CD45-positive, BCL6-positive and CD15/CD30-negative, unlike the Reed-Sternberg cells of classic disease
Most patients are men presenting with localised, indolent peripheral lymphadenopathy, often cervical, axillary or inguinal, and B symptoms are uncommon at diagnosis
The clinical course is indolent with a tendency to late relapse, so prolonged follow-up is required
Early-stage disease is often managed with radiotherapy alone or limited chemoimmunotherapy, with anti-CD20 targeted agents playing a useful role given CD20 expression
There is a recognised risk of transformation to an aggressive large B-cell lymphoma, so re-biopsy of rapidly enlarging or discordant nodes is important
Histological growth patterns showing a more diffuse or T-cell-rich architecture carry a higher risk of relapse and transformation
reference.pathophysiology: The tumour arises from a germinal-centre B cell that has undergone clonal transformation, giving rise to the characteristic large LP (popcorn) cell with a multilobated nucleus. Unlike classic Hodgkin lymphoma, these cells preserve much of the mature B-cell transcriptional programme and continue to express B-cell antigens and surface immunoglobulin machinery. They reside within expanded nodular meshworks of follicular dendritic cells surrounded by small reactive B lymphocytes and a rosetting rim of T cells. This retained B-cell identity underlies both the CD20 positivity that makes the tumour amenable to anti-CD20 targeting and the propensity, in some cases, to progress to a diffuse aggressive large B-cell lymphoma.
additionalDifferentials: Classic Hodgkin lymphoma, particularly the lymphocyte-rich subtype
additionalInvestigations: Excisional lymph node biopsy for architecture, which is essential as fine-needle aspiration is inadequate
Immunohistochemistry demonstrating CD20-positive, CD45-positive, BCL6-positive, CD15/CD30-negative LP cells
Assessment of the background T-cell rosettes and follicular dendritic meshwork pattern
PET-CT for staging and detection of possible transformation
Bone marrow evaluation in selected advanced or symptomatic cases
Baseline blood counts, lactate dehydrogenase and organ function testing
redFlags: A rapidly enlarging or fixed nodal mass suggesting transformation to aggressive large B-cell lymphoma
New B symptoms, bulky disease or extranodal spread after an indolent course
Discordant histology between sites on staging imaging warranting re-biopsy
Rising lactate dehydrogenase with clinical deterioration
reference.prognosis: Early-stage disease has an excellent long-term outlook with high cure rates, but the indolent behaviour is offset by a tendency to late relapse and a small but real risk of transformation to aggressive large B-cell lymphoma, which worsens prognosis and mandates long-term surveillance.
pitfalls: Misclassifying the tumour as classic Hodgkin lymphoma and thereby selecting inappropriate therapy
Relying on fine-needle aspiration, which cannot demonstrate the diagnostic nodular architecture
Overlooking a variant (diffuse or T-cell-rich) growth pattern that predicts higher relapse risk
Failing to re-biopsy a discordant or rapidly growing node and missing transformation
Assuming cure after early remission and abandoning long-term follow-up
references: British Society for Haematology guidance on Hodgkin lymphoma
management: Managed as a distinct entity from classical Hodgkin lymphoma because of its indolent course and retained CD20 expression on the lymphocyte-predominant popcorn cells
Localised, non-bulky stage I-II disease is commonly managed with involved-site radiotherapy alone, without systemic chemotherapy
When a solitary involved node has been completely excised, a period of observation without further treatment is a recognised option in some cases

Advanced-stage or symptomatic disease is treated with systemic therapy using anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody therapy alone or combined with a multi-agent chemotherapy backbone, followed by consolidative radiotherapy to residual or bulky sites when indicated

Relapsed or refractory disease is treated with retreatment using anti-CD20 antibody therapy or chemoimmunotherapy, with more intensive approaches such as autologous stem cell transplantation reserved for select transformed or heavily pretreated cases
Transformation to aggressive large B-cell lymphoma is managed as de novo aggressive large B-cell lymphoma with anthracycline-based combination chemoimmunotherapy
Excisional biopsy is required for diagnosis since architecture cannot be assessed on needle sampling, and in a fully excised solitary node it can also serve a treatment role

Radiotherapy is the mainstay for localised disease and, in advanced-stage disease, is used as consolidation for residual masses after chemotherapy, with benefit concentrated in patients without a complete response
Combination chemotherapy is reserved for higher-volume, advanced, or symptomatic disease rather than used routinely for localised disease
Prolonged clinical follow-up beyond timeframes typical for classical Hodgkin lymphoma is appropriate given the indolent course and tendency to late relapse
A low threshold to re-biopsy is warranted for any node that enlarges rapidly, becomes symptomatic, or behaves atypically for indolent disease, given the risk of transformation
Long-term survivorship care should attend to late treatment effects from radiotherapy fields and cumulative systemic therapy exposure
Refer to a haematology specialist and a centre with lymphoma pathology expertise at diagnosis to distinguish this entity from classical Hodgkin lymphoma and its mimics
Refer to radiation oncology for radiotherapy planning in localised disease and to medical oncology or haematology for systemic therapy in advanced or relapsed disease
